questions.q: What are the three sections every real migration guide covers, in the order they typically get harder to resolve automatically?
options: Procedural code, data type mapping tables, unsupported functions
Indexes, constraints, and storage settings
Data type mapping tables, unsupported/different functions, procedural code
Backup strategy, network configuration, user permissions
questions.explain: Guides move from the most mechanical concern (type mapping) to functions to the hardest part, procedural code, which is why that order matches increasing manual effort.

questions.q: What does AWS Schema Conversion Tool's assessment report actually tell you?
options: A list of which users have permission to run the migration
What percentage of objects converted automatically, plus an explicit list of action items it couldn't convert
Only whether the migration succeeded or failed, with no detail
The exact dollar cost of running the target database
questions.explain: SCT's assessment report is built specifically to separate what converted cleanly from what needs manual rework, flagged as action items.

questions.q: Which tool is Oracle's own built-in migration tool, accessed inside SQL Developer?
options: AWS Schema Conversion Tool
The Migration Workbench (Tools -> Migration)
The Data Migration Assistant
Azure Database Migration Service
questions.explain: SQL Developer ships with a Migration Workbench that connects to a source database, captures its schema, and generates equivalent Oracle objects.

questions.q: Why is the procedural code section consistently the hardest part of any real migration, according to this lesson?
options: Procedural code is always written incorrectly in the source system
Procedural dialects diverge the most of anything covered in this course, so tools can't safely guess intent every time
Vendors deliberately leave procedural code undocumented
Procedural code never needs to be migrated at all
questions.explain: Chapters 5-8 showed real, structural differences in error handling, packages, and cursors across platforms -- differences too specific for an automated tool to resolve alone every time.

questions.q: In a data type mapping table entry like 'DATETIME2 -> TIMESTAMP,' what should you check before trusting an automatic conversion?
options: Whether the table has a primary key
The 'note' column, such as whether the fractional-seconds precision actually maps 1:1
Only the column name, never the type
Nothing -- mapping table entries are always exact matches
questions.explain: Mapping tables list a target type plus a note for exactly this reason -- precision, range, or length details often keep a mapping from being a clean 1:1 swap.
